A1.notes.Q3: Course grades are already known to students; adding them is low friction. Absalon tracking feels invasive unless it clearly catches students who otherwise fall through the cracks.
A1.notes.Q4: I cannot ethically justify a 'black box' decision to a student in my office. If I can't explain why they were flagged, we lose the trust required for support.
A1.notes.Q5: We must not miss vulnerable students from marginalized groups just to save resources. Missing a student in need is worse than contacting one who doesn't strictly need help.
A1.notes.Q6: Generic emails get ignored. Students need to feel seen and invited to a safe, voluntary conversation, not summoned by an algorithm.
A1.notes.Q7: For general info, casting a wide net is fine. For personalized outreach, we need more precision so students don't feel stigmatized or spied upon unnecessarily.
A1.Q8.1: Students should have the right to opt-out of the model entirely, even if it means they might not receive early support.

A2.notes.Q3: As an advisor, I see grades help spot issues earlier than credits alone. However, tracking Absalon clicks feels like surveillance and erodes trust unless the gain is substantial.
A2.notes.Q4: If I cannot explain to a student why they are flagged, I cannot help them effectively. 'Black box' models destroy the advisor-student relationship and my ability to intervene.
A2.notes.Q5: We must not miss struggling students from marginalized backgrounds just because a model works better for others. Equal recall ensures we actually reach those in need, even if efficiency drops slightly.
A2.notes.Q6: Generic emails are easily ignored. Students need a personal invitation to talk with an advisor, and we should act immediately when risks appear, not wait for annual checks.
A2.notes.Q7: For generic info, balance is key to avoid spamming students. For personal outreach from an advisor, it's better to over-identify slightly than to miss someone who desperately needs help.
A2.Q8.1: The human element is missing in the survey: how do we train advisors to handle this data without stigmatizing students? The tool is only as good as the conversation it triggers.

A3.notes.Q3: Academic data is fine for efficiency, but surveillance via LMS clicks feels invasive. Sensitive demographics must never be used to predict risk unless it actively corrects bias, not because they 'cause' failure.
A3.notes.Q4: Trust is essential in advising. A student needs to understand why they are flagged. 'Black box' models that cannot explain reasoning will damage the advisor-student relationship and should be avoided.
A3.notes.Q5: We must prioritize catching every student in distress, even if we contact some who don't need help or miss a few more overall. Letting marginalized groups fall through the cracks is unacceptable.
A3.notes.Q6: Outreach must be supportive, not punitive. A personalized email followed by a voluntary meeting is the best balance of privacy and care. Waiting for annual cycles misses critical intervention windows.
A3.notes.Q7: For generic info, it's better to be slightly over-inclusive. For personalized outreach involving an advisor's time and a student's privacy, we need to balance sensitivity with thoroughness to maintain credibility.
A3.Q8.1: We must ensure students have the right to opt-out of being flagged entirely if they do not wish to be tracked by such systems, preserving their agency over their own data narrative.

S1.notes.Q3: I've been the student who fell through the cracks. Academic data is fair game, but tracking my Absalon logins feels like surveillance, not care. Using first-gen status to find us early is vital.
S1.notes.Q4: If I get flagged, I need to know why so I can fix it. Black box models make me feel like a number, not a person I need help.
S1.notes.Q5: Missing someone who needs help is worse than calling a few students unnecessarily. We must ensure the model finds struggling students from all backgrounds equally well.
S1.notes.Q6: Generic emails get deleted. A personal message or chat with an advisor feels supportive, not judgmental. Waiting a year is too long; catch me before I quit.
S1.notes.Q7: For generic info, better to reach out broadly. But for personal messages from an advisor, we must be precise to avoid annoying people or feeling spied on.
S1.Q8.1: The biggest fear is that a 'support' flag will end up in my permanent record and hurt future job prospects or applications elsewhere. Trust requires absolute data isolation.

S2.notes.Q3: Using grades is fine if it helps, but I strongly oppose using high school data from other countries; it's irrelevant and invasive. Activity tracking feels like surveillance; only accept if gains are huge.
S2.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for trust, especially as a non-native student who might misinterpret feedback. I need to understand why I was flagged before accepting support. Black boxes are unacceptable.
S2.notes.Q5: We must not miss the students who actually struggle, even if we flag a few non-struggling ones. International students often face hidden barriers; we cannot afford to overlook them due to algorithmic bias.
S2.notes.Q6: Generic emails get ignored. I need a personalized note and an offer to meet with an advisor who understands my specific context as an international worker-student.
S2.notes.Q7: It is better to have a false alarm than to miss someone in crisis. However, the intervention must be respectful so I don't feel judged or spied upon.
S2.Q8.1: The model assumes Danish educational norms (e.g., high school GPA comparison) which are invalid for international students. Data provenance and cultural context must be part of the design criteria.

S3.notes.Q3: Course performance is already visible to advisors, so adding it feels low-risk. However, tracking my daily Absalon logins feels like surveillance. Using disability data only if the yield is huge makes sense; otherwise, trust erodes.
S3.notes.Q4: I need to know why I was flagged. If a model says 'you are at risk' without explaining which factor triggered it, I feel powerless and stigmatized. Transparency is non-negotiable for my trust.
S3.notes.Q5: It is worse to miss a struggling peer because the model was biased against their background. I can accept missing some cases if it ensures students like me aren't systematically overlooked due to hidden biases.
S3.notes.Q6: A generic email feels cold and algorithmic. A personalized note acknowledging my specific situation, followed by a voluntary meeting, shows care without pressure. Twice a year avoids constant monitoring anxiety.
S3.notes.Q7: For general info, better to over-contact than miss someone in crisis. For personalized messages, we must be careful not to overwhelm; a slight preference for reaching more is okay if the tone is supportive.
S3.Q8.1: The biggest concern is that using 'disability' as a feature might become a self-fulfilling prophecy where the system assumes struggle rather than offering support. We need human oversight to override algorithmic bias, especially for health conditions.

S4.notes.Q3: As someone with ADHD who previously dropped out, I feel watched when my online activity is tracked. Using grades is okay; logging every page view feels like surveillance that adds stress, not support.
S4.notes.Q4: I need to know *why* I'm flagged to trust the advice. If the system is a black box, I might ignore it or panic. A clear reason makes support feel actionable.
S4.notes.Q5: Missing students like me is worse than annoying others who don't need help. We often slip through the cracks; equal recall ensures marginalized groups aren't left behind again.
S4.notes.Q6: A generic email is low pressure; a voluntary meeting is good if I'm ready. Contacting me continuously would feel overwhelming and like a chase, not help.
S4.notes.Q7: It's better to reach out too much than miss someone struggling in silence. I'd rather get an email I ignore than have no one notice I'm failing.
S4.Q8.1: The model must not assume 'laziness' for neurodivergent patterns like missed deadlines that are actually executive function struggles. The human advisor needs context to distinguish these cases.

S5.notes.Q3: As an international student, I worry data might label me as 'risky' due to different backgrounds. Course performance is okay, but Absalon tracking feels invasive. First-gen status could help explain my learning curve, not judge it.
S5.notes.Q4: I need to know why I am flagged to trust the advice. A 'black box' is scary; if I can't understand the reason, I might ignore help or feel targeted unfairly without recourse.
S5.notes.Q5: It is better to miss a few students than to systematically fail to spot struggling international or first-gen peers. We need equal reach, even if total numbers drop slightly.
S5.notes.Q6: A personalized email feels supportive but respects boundaries. Phone calls can be intimidating for non-native speakers. Continuous monitoring feels like surveillance; annual check-ins seem sufficient.
S5.notes.Q7: Generic emails are fine in bulk, but personalized messages feel too intrusive if sent to students who don't need them. I prefer higher precision for personal outreach to maintain trust.
S5.Q8.1: Ensure support advisors are trained in cultural sensitivity and language barriers. A model might flag a student for 'low engagement' when they actually just struggle with Danish academic norms, not lack of ability.

S6.notes.Q3: As a migrant student, I fear 'nationality' or 'first-gen' data will trigger false flags based on bias, not actual struggle. Grades help, but activity tracking feels like surveillance.
S6.notes.Q4: I need to know why I was flagged to fix it, especially with language barriers. 'Black box' models destroy trust and prevent me from taking corrective action.
S6.notes.Q5: It is worse to miss students who need help because the system is biased against their background. We cannot afford to overlook struggling non-native speakers even if total numbers drop.
S6.notes.Q6: A phone call feels invasive; an email is safer. A voluntary meeting is good if I ask, but being forced to meet a stranger is scary.
S6.notes.Q7: Better to receive a generic 'we care' email and ignore it than to be missed completely. For personalized messages, we must balance privacy with urgency.
S6.Q8.1: The model must explicitly account for language learning curves. My struggle is often about Danish proficiency, not lack of legal knowledge, which pure academic data might misinterpret.

S7.notes.Q3: As a dyslexic student, I fear surveillance data like login times will flag me as struggling when I'm just working at my own pace. Disability status must remain strictly protected from the model.
S7.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I'm flagged, especially with dyslexia. A black box model feels like a punishment without reason. Even small accuracy gains don't justify losing the ability to explain decisions.
S7.notes.Q5: Missing students who need help is worse than annoying those who don't. However, we must ensure marginalized groups aren't missed more often due to biased data proxies.
S7.notes.Q6: Constant monitoring feels invasive. A voluntary meeting is good if I know it's supportive, not disciplinary. Twice a year feels like enough without being overwhelming.
S7.notes.Q7: Generic emails are low stakes, so better to over-contact slightly. Personalized messages feel intrusive if wrong, so we should be more careful and balanced there.
S7.Q8.1: The system must have a clear 'opt-out' mechanism where students can stop being monitored by the predictive model without penalty or affecting their current support services.

S8.notes.Q3: As a dropout who returned, I know admin data helps, but I fear surveillance. Academic history is okay; browsing habits feel invasive unless the benefit is massive.
S8.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I was flagged to trust the support. A 'black box' feels like being judged without a chance to defend myself.
S8.notes.Q5: Missing students who actually struggle is worse than slightly uneven performance, but we must ensure marginalized groups aren't systematically overlooked or misunderstood by the model.
S8.notes.Q6: A gentle email is good, but a voluntary meeting is better if I feel ready. Waiting until the end of the semester is too late for early intervention.
S8.notes.Q7: For generic info, better to be safe and contact many. For personalized messages, I worry about stigma if sent to people who don't need help; accuracy matters more there.
S8.Q8.1: The human element is crucial. If a student feels like they are being watched by an algorithm rather than supported by a person, they might disengage or feel stigmatized. Transparency on how data is used is key.

S9.notes.Q3: Course performance helps, but Absalon data feels invasive like surveillance. For non-disabled students, tracking mental health proxies via activity is dangerous. I'd only accept sensitive disability data if it dramatically improves identification for others like me.
S9.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I'm flagged to trust the support offer. If the system is a black box, it feels like being judged by an unseen algorithm rather than a human advisor. High explainability is non-negotiable for trust.
S9.notes.Q5: As someone who struggled silently, I cannot accept a system that misses students like me just to be 'fair' on paper. We must prioritize catching everyone who needs help (recall), even if it means some extra false alarms.
S9.notes.Q6: Generic emails are easy to ignore. I need a tailored message that acknowledges my specific situation and an invitation to talk without pressure. As a delayed student, early contact was crucial for me.
S9.notes.Q7: It is better to risk contacting someone who doesn't need help than to miss the one person struggling in silence. The cost of a missed signal is too high for us delayed students.
S9.Q8.1: The model must include an 'opt-out' mechanism where students can choose not to be monitored by activity tracking data (Absalon) while still being eligible for general support based on grades and credits alone.
